claimsMade.nodeLabel: DoD OIG - Evaluation of the DoD's Actions Regarding Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (DODIG-2023-109)
claimsMade.text: Recommendation 1: 'We recommend that the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security, in coordination with the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office Director, issue a Department of Defense policy to integrate unidentified anomalous phenomena roles, responsibilities, requirements, and coordination procedures into existing intelligence, counterintelligence, and force protection policies and procedures. The policy should include methods to address unidentified anomalous phenomena incidents and should align with policies and procedures for the protection of United States persons' civil liberties.' USD(I&S) and the AARO Director agreed; the recommendation was left 'resolved but open'.

claimsMade.text: Historical framing in the summary: 'Over the past decades, the DoD has initiated infrequent and inconclusive efforts to identify and understand the origin, capabilities, and intent of unidentified aerial phenomena (UAP)... the DoD has relied heavily on the Services and Components to detect, report, collect, analyze, and identify UAP since the 1940s.' It counts 243 sightings investigated under PROJECT SIGN (1947-1949) and 'over 12,000 reported sightings' under PROJECT BLUE BOOK (1952-1969).

claimsMade.text: On the absence of a response plan: 'The DoD has not issued a comprehensive UAP response plan that identifies roles, responsibilities, requirements, and coordination procedures... As a result, the DoD response to UAP incidents is uncoordinated and concentrated within each Military Department. Officials from the Military Services and MDCOs stated that they have been waiting for the DoD to issue comprehensive UAP guidance before developing their own guidance.'

desc: The DoD Office of Inspector General is the Department's statutory internal watchdog, created by the Inspector General Act, and it is the body that produced the only formal audit of the Department's UAP conduct. On 15 August 2023 - three weeks after David Grusch's testimony - the DoD OIG issued DODIG-2023-109, 'Evaluation of the DoD's Actions Regarding Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena', whose stated objective was to determine 'how the DoD, military services, defense agencies, and military department counterintelligence organizations took intelligence, counterintelligence, and force protection actions to detect, report, collect, analyze, and identify UAP'. The report itself is classified; only an unclassified summary was released, and the OIG issued a press release on 25 January 2024. The OIG is also the office to which Luis Elizondo submitted a complaint in May 2021 alleging reprisal and mishandling. The structural point for this board is that DoD OIG is subject to the same access architecture as everyone else: an inspector general who is not read into a waived unacknowledged special access program cannot audit it, and DODIG-2023-109's classified status means the public cannot determine whether the audit reached the SAP enterprise at all.
